name: Zoe Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brookside Farm for Alun and Meg Pryce. They rent it, about 400 ewes, a few dozen suckler cows, and wheat and oilseed rape on the flatter fields. My day starts at seven with the hens, then feeding the cattle in winter, checking sheep, and whatever Alun shouts across the yard. At lambing I do nights, which I actually love.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did twenty-two years in a care home, lifting and washing and holding hands at the end. At 55 my shoulder went and I thought, if I'm going to be tired, I want to be tired outside. Meg is a friend from chapel choir, and she said they needed a pair of hands, so here I am, three years in and still learning which end of a ewe to look at.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the lambs, obviously, and being outside when the light comes up over the hill. What wears me out is not knowing things. Alun will say check the ewe for twin lamb disease and I'll have to ask him what that looks like, again. Sometimes I ask the chatbot on my phone in the evening so I don't look daft the next day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now the money and attention go back into things that matter, like care homes and rural buses. At Brookside it wouldn't change much. Online I'd probably share something funny about all the people who bet their houses on robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means life carries on. Dev, my husband, keeps his post round, I keep my hens and ewes, and we get to retirement at a normal pace. The only cloud is that Brookside's tenancy comes up for renewal in 2029, but Alun reckons the landlord's happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd put a bit more into the savings each month, maybe seventy-five, so we've got a proper six months by the time I stop at 64. And I'd keep asking the chatbot my daft sheep questions, because it does help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Content, even. I'd be a bit smug about all the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tenancy comes up in 2029. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, but only a little. Alun and Meg have been there thirty years and they pay on time. If the landlord sold up it would be a different story, but I've no reason to think so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good last few years of work look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lambing every spring, Dev's tea on the table, and one week in the caravan each summer. I'd love to get good enough that Alun stops checking my work. My ambition at 58 is to be trusted with the ewes on my own, without the farmer checking my work.

say: Good: maybe the money and attention go back into **care homes** and rural buses instead.
At Brookside **nothing much changes**, and I'd laugh at people who bet their houses on robots.
think: Life carries on: Dev keeps his **post round**, I keep my ewes, and we reach retirement normally.
The one cloud is Brookside's **tenancy renewal** in 2029, though the landlord seems happy.
do: Keep working the **hens and ewes** at Brookside as I do now.
Save an extra **seventy-five a month** to reach six months' cover by 64.
Keep using the **chatbot** in the evenings to learn the sheep diseases Alun mentions.
feel: **Calm** and content, even a little **smug** about all the fuss.
S0.quote: My ambition at 58 is to be trusted with the ewes on my own, without the farmer checking my work.
fieldNote: She came to farming from **care work** and finds the outdoor work freeing rather than hard.
Her only real worry, the **2029 tenancy**, she dismisses quickly and with reasons.
She already uses a **chatbot** quietly to cover gaps in her knowledge.

steps.text: Keep doing the hens, feeding and lambing nights at Brookside
Save an extra 75 a month towards six months' cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after the people whose jobs get eaten, like Joel, my son, who answers phones for an energy company. At work I'd say the farm's probably fine for a while. Online I'd share petitions for retraining money, that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, not much at first. Alun's paperwork, the movement records and ordering, might go to an AI, and he'd be thrilled. What worries me is Joel's call centre and the way Dev's sorting office keeps cutting shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the short course the farmers' group runs on the new sheep-weighing and records app, so I'm useful when Alun gets it. I'd keep working as normal. And I'd sit Joel down and help him look at the electrician's apprenticeship, because his call-centre job will shrink first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for myself, but I can feel the ground shifting. It's like the morning before a storm when the ewes all go quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Dev's shifts were cut, what would that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose maybe a fifth of his pay, and that's the car repairs and the caravan week. We'd manage, but my savings plan would slow down. I'd probably pick up an extra Saturday at Brookside if Alun had the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more yourself in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once Meg and the others at choir are using it, yes. I'm not one to be first, but I'm not daft either. If a sheep app tells me a ewe is losing weight before I can see it, that's a lamb saved.

say: We must look after people whose jobs get eaten, like my son Joel at a **call centre**.
I'd share petitions for **retraining money**, and say farms are probably fine for a while.
think: Alun's **paperwork** goes to AI first, which leaves my hands-on work alone for now.
The real worry is Joel's job and Dev's **sorting-office shifts** being cut.
do: Take the farmers' group **short course** on the sheep-weighing and records app.
Help Joel look into an **electrician's apprenticeship** before his call-centre job shrinks.
Offer to work an **extra Saturday** at Brookside if Dev's shifts are cut.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the quiet before a storm, though not scared for my own job.
S1.quote: If a sheep app tells me a ewe is losing weight before I can see it, that's a lamb saved.
fieldNote: Her fear is for **family members** in desk and sorting jobs more than for herself.
She'll adopt tech **once peers do**, and frames it in terms of animal welfare.
A cut to **Dev's pay** would slow savings but not break the household.

steps.text: Take the farmers' group course on the sheep records app
Help son Joel apply for an electrician's apprenticeship
Keep working at Brookside and add Saturdays if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is far too fast, and the government has to step in with real money for people, not just a website. At work I'd say what everyone would say: who's going to milk, lamb, feed, if not us? Online I'd be angry, I think, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 Alun's whole office side goes to the AI, which is fine. But robots by 2031 means I'm 63 and the sheep-checking and feeding could go. I'd planned to stop at 64, so I'd lose a year, maybe two, of pay, and Dev's sorting would go even sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd squeeze another hundred a month into savings. I'd join the farmworkers' union, which I've never bothered with, because we'd need someone negotiating. And I'd tell Amira we can't help with her house deposit after all, which would break my heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see it coming but I can't stop it. It makes my chest tight thinking of Dev coming home with a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Amira when you told her about the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Amira that her dad and I need to look after ourselves first, just for a few years. She'd understand; she's a teacher, she's sensible. But I'd feel like I'd let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join a union. What would you want it to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get older farmworkers a fair exit: some pay, some notice, maybe a chance to stay on and watch the robots. I don't expect miracles. I just don't want Alun to have to choose between us and the farm.

say: This is **far too fast**, and government must put real money behind people, not websites.
Who will milk, lamb and feed if not us? I'd be **angry online**, which isn't like me.
think: Robots by **2031** mean I lose a year or two of pay before my planned stop at 64.
Dev's **sorting job** could go even sooner, since thinking AI arrives in 2028.
do: Squeeze another **hundred a month** into savings, starting now.
Join the **farmworkers' union** for the first time so someone negotiates for us.
Tell Amira we can't help with her **house deposit** for a few years.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest picturing Dev coming home with a letter.
**Guilty** about letting Amira down on the deposit.
S2.quote: I'd tell my daughter Amira that her dad and I need to look after ourselves first, just for a few years.
fieldNote: The short warning time turns her **steady plan** to retire at 64 into a one- or two-year gap.
Two incomes at risk: **Dev's sorting** under thinking AI, hers under robots three years later.
Joining a union is a real **shift** for someone who never bothered before.

steps.text: Put another 100 a month into savings
Join the farmworkers' union for the first time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them and stop arguing about whether it's real. At the chapel coffee morning I'd say the same. Online I'd share things about pensions and retraining, because that's where people need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be mostly out of it. Robots in 2034 means I'm 66, and I'll have stopped at 64. The 2031 AGI would change Alun's planning and ordering, but the ewes still need my hands till I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as planned, lambing every spring, and stop at 64. I'd still add a bit to savings, fifty a month, as a cushion. And I'd vote for whoever promises to keep the state pension safe and pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for Dev and the children than for me. I'm lucky on timing, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Dev's job last until he retires in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev is 61 and wants to go at 66, so probably just about. The sorting machines have been taking bits of his job for years. My husband Dev jokes that he'll retire from the post office the same week the robot postman starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about being lucky on timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit guilty, if I'm honest. Meg's nephew is 30 and works with Alun three days a week. I'd worry about that boy far more than about myself.

say: We have **five years**, so let's use them instead of arguing about whether it's real.
People need help with **pensions and retraining**, so that's what I'd share.
think: With robots in **2034** I'm 66 and already retired at 64, so I'm mostly out of it.
AGI in 2031 changes Alun's **planning and ordering**, but the ewes still need my hands.
do: Keep working **lambing seasons** at Brookside and stop at 64 as planned.
Add **fifty a month** to savings as a small extra cushion.
Vote for whoever protects the **state pension** and pays for retraining.
feel: **Uneasy** for Dev and the children, and a little **guilty** about my lucky timing.
S3.quote: My husband Dev jokes that he'll retire from the post office the same week the robot postman starts.
fieldNote: Five years' warning lets her **retire on time**, which she recognises as luck.
Concern moves to **younger workers** like Meg's nephew.
She ties her vote to **pensions and retraining**, in keeping with her progressive views.

steps.text: Keep lambing at Brookside and stop at 64
Vote for parties protecting the state pension and retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. At choir I'd tell the younger ones to plan now. Online I'd probably share the odd article and then go back to photos of lambs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It hardly touches me. I'll be retired by the time the 2036 AI arrives, and the robots in 2039 come when I'm 71. My worry is just that the kids get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as planned and enjoy the last six springs. I'd use the farm app more as it gets better, because I'd like to leave Alun with good records. That's about all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Almost peaceful. It's somebody else's storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have learned before you stop at 64?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to be able to do a whole lambing on my own, with Alun asleep for once. And I'd want to know the records system well enough to train whoever comes after me. That would feel like a proper finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this future you'd look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the grandchildren won't have to do jobs that wreck their shoulders like mine. If robots do the heavy lifting in care homes, good, but I hope people still get to hold hands at the end.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it.
I'd tell the **younger ones** at choir to start planning now.
think: I'll be **retired** before the 2036 AI, and 71 when robots arrive in 2039.
My only worry is that my **children** get through it.
do: Carry on as planned and **enjoy the last** six lambing springs at Brookside.
Use the **farm records app** more so Alun is left with good records.
feel: **Calm**, almost peaceful, because it's somebody else's storm.
S4.quote: If robots do the heavy lifting in care homes, good, but I hope people still get to hold hands at the end.
fieldNote: With a **decade of warning** she sees no risk to her own work or income.
Her **care-home past** shapes what she hopes robots will and won't do.
Her goal is a **proper finish**: running a lambing alone and training a successor.

steps.text: Work out the last six lambing seasons at Brookside
Learn the farm records app well enough to train a successor

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where Dev and I could both lose work before we're ready, and the kids too. What would help is a proper bridge for older workers, some money and notice, and Alun being able to keep a couple of us on without losing the farm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about care. Everybody talks about robots on farms, but I spent twenty-two years in a care home, and I learned one thing there. A machine can lift a person out of bed, but it can't sit with them. Somebody should ask the old folk what they want.

headlineQuote: A machine can lift a person out of bed, but it can't sit with them.
portrait: Zoe is a **58-year-old farmhand** at Brookside, three years in after twenty-two years of care-home work.
She's steady with technology, quietly using a **chatbot** to learn sheep diseases and willing to adopt tools once friends do.
Her worries centre on **Dev's sorting job** and her son Joel's call-centre work more than her own.
She stays calm or uneasy in most scenarios, but turns **anxious** in AGI by 2028, which cuts her working years short.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Dev could both lose work before they're ready to retire.
whatWouldHelp: A **bridge** for older workers with money and notice, so Alun can keep some staff without **losing the farm**.
